items.guideline: DailyMed sertraline prescribing information, bleeding warning
items.scenario: A 30-year-old woman takes sertraline 50 mg by mouth daily for anxiety and lorazepam 0.5 mg by mouth at bedtime as needed. She started ibuprofen 600 mg by mouth three times daily for knee pain. She has no history of gastrointestinal bleeding.
items.question: Which paired regimen poses the greatest risk?
options: Sertraline 50 mg daily with a combined oral contraceptive
Sertraline 50 mg daily with ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily
Lorazepam 0.5 mg at bedtime with cetirizine 10 mg daily
Sertraline 50 mg daily with lorazepam 0.5 mg at bedtime as needed
items.correctAnswer: Sertraline 50 mg daily with ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily
items.explanation: Sertraline 50 mg daily plus ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily is the greatest risk. SSRIs reduce platelet serotonin and NSAIDs injure the gastric lining, and the sertraline label warns of more gastrointestinal bleeding with NSAIDs, aspirin, or anticoagulants. Lorazepam 0.5 mg at bedtime may add sedation but has no bleeding warning and is a usual adjunct. Cetirizine 10 mg daily with that lorazepam dose causes only mild sedation. Sertraline does not reduce the effect of a combined oral contraceptive. Takeaway: an NSAID, not low-dose bedtime lorazepam, is the sertraline interaction to avoid or cover.

items.guideline: ACG Clinical Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (2022); FDA ranitidine market removal (2020)
items.scenario: A 40-year-old woman has heartburn at least 3 days a week for 2 months. She had taken OTC ranitidine until products containing it were removed from the market. She has no trouble swallowing, bleeding, weight loss, or vomiting, and she is not pregnant.
items.question: Which recommendation is most appropriate now?
options: Calcium carbonate 750 mg by mouth only after meals
Famotidine 10 mg by mouth once daily as needed
Omeprazole 20 mg by mouth once daily before breakfast for 8 weeks
Ask her to restart ranitidine 150 mg by mouth twice daily
items.correctAnswer: Omeprazole 20 mg by mouth once daily before breakfast for 8 weeks
items.explanation: Omeprazole 20 mg once daily before breakfast for 8 weeks is appropriate for heartburn on 3 or more days a week. The ACG GERD guideline uses a once-daily PPI for frequent symptoms, taken before a meal. The FDA asked manufacturers to withdraw all ranitidine in 2020 because of NDMA, so it cannot be restarted. Famotidine 10 mg once daily as needed is too little for symptoms this frequent. Calcium carbonate after meals only neutralizes acid briefly and does not heal frequent GERD. Takeaway: frequent heartburn gets a once-daily PPI; ranitidine stays off the market.

items.guideline: DailyMed phenytoin prescribing information, therapeutic range and nonlinear kinetics
items.scenario: A 30-year-old man takes phenytoin 300 mg by mouth daily, as 100 mg three times daily, for epilepsy. Seizures have increased. The total phenytoin level is 8 mcg/mL and albumin is 4.2 g/dL. He started omeprazole 20 mg daily for GERD one week ago.
items.question: Which action best addresses the increased seizures?
options: Stop omeprazole and keep phenytoin at 300 mg daily
Add levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily and keep phenytoin at 300 mg daily
Switch omeprazole to famotidine 20 mg twice daily and keep phenytoin at 300 mg daily
Increase phenytoin to 330 mg daily and recheck the level in 7 days
items.correctAnswer: Increase phenytoin to 330 mg daily and recheck the level in 7 days
items.explanation: A total phenytoin level of 8 mcg/mL is below the usual 10–20 mcg/mL range, and albumin 4.2 g/dL means the total level is interpretable. Phenytoin is nonlinear, so raise the dose by 30 mg, to 330 mg daily, and recheck in 7 days rather than jumping to 400 mg. Omeprazole can raise phenytoin levels; stopping it or switching to famotidine 20 mg twice daily does not correct a level of 8. Adding levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily leaves the subtherapeutic phenytoin untreated. Takeaway: a level of 8 mcg/mL needs a small phenytoin increase and a repeat level, not an H2-blocker swap.

items.topic: COPD exacerbations on LAMA with low eosinophils
items.scenario: A 55-year-old man with COPD uses tiotropium 18 mcg inhaled once daily and albuterol 90 mcg, 2 inhalations every 4 to 6 hours as needed. He has had 2 exacerbations this year, neither requiring hospitalization. The blood eosinophil count is 80 cells/µL. He is not asthmatic.
items.question: Which change best reduces further exacerbations?
options: Add montelukast 10 mg by mouth daily
Add theophylline 300 mg by mouth daily
Add fluticasone/salmeterol 250/50 mcg, 1 inhalation twice daily
Switch to tiotropium/olodaterol 2.5/2.5 mcg, 2 inhalations once daily
items.correctAnswer: Switch to tiotropium/olodaterol 2.5/2.5 mcg, 2 inhalations once daily
items.explanation: On tiotropium alone with exacerbations and eosinophils of 80 cells/µL, GOLD 2026 calls for a LAMA plus a LABA. Tiotropium/olodaterol 2.5/2.5 mcg, 2 inhalations once daily, supplies that pair; stop the separate tiotropium so he does not take two LAMAs. An ICS is reserved for eosinophils of at least 300 cells/µL, or at least 100 when exacerbations continue, so fluticasone/salmeterol 250/50 mcg twice daily adds pneumonia risk without an eosinophil indication. Montelukast 10 mg daily has no COPD role. Theophylline 300 mg daily is a narrow-index last resort. Takeaway: low eosinophils mean LAMA/LABA, not an ICS/LABA.

items.scenario: A 62-year-old man with COPD uses tiotropium 18 mcg inhaled once daily and albuterol as needed. Dyspnea is worse and he uses the rescue inhaler daily. FEV1 is 55% predicted. He has had no exacerbation in the past year. The blood eosinophil count is 90 cells/µL.
items.question: Which inhaler should replace tiotropium monotherapy?
options: Budesonide/formoterol 160/4.5 mcg, 2 inhalations twice daily
Umeclidinium/vilanterol 62.5/25 mcg, 1 inhalation once daily
Ipratropium 17 mcg, 2 inhalations four times daily
Montelukast 10 mg by mouth daily, with tiotropium continued
items.explanation: Dyspnea on a LAMA, with eosinophils of 90 cells/µL and no recent exacerbation, is treated by adding a LABA. Umeclidinium/vilanterol 62.5/25 mcg, 1 inhalation once daily, is a LAMA/LABA and replaces tiotropium so two LAMAs are not combined. GOLD 2026 does not add an ICS for dyspnea alone at this eosinophil count, so budesonide/formoterol 160/4.5 mcg, 2 inhalations twice daily, is the wrong escalation. Ipratropium four times daily duplicates anticholinergic effect and is short-acting. Montelukast 10 mg daily is not COPD therapy. Takeaway: dyspnea on tiotropium gets a LAMA/LABA, not an ICS/LABA.

items.scenario: S.G. is a 34-year-old woman who had a traumatic splenectomy 14 days ago. Records show no adult Tdap and no pneumococcal, meningococcal, or Hib vaccine. She is not pregnant. Influenza vaccine is in season.
items.question: Which vaccines should the pharmacist give today? Select all that apply.
options: PCV20 0.5 mL IM once, with no PPSV23 after it
MenACWY 0.5 mL IM now and again in 8 weeks, then a booster every 5 years, plus a MenB series
Inactivated influenza vaccine 0.5 mL IM once this season
Recombinant zoster vaccine 0.5 mL IM now and again in 2 to 6 months because of asplenia
Tdap 0.5 mL IM once, plus Hib 0.5 mL IM once
items.correctAnswer: PCV20 0.5 mL IM once, with no PPSV23 after it|||MenACWY 0.5 mL IM now and again in 8 weeks, then a booster every 5 years, plus a MenB series|||Inactivated influenza vaccine 0.5 mL IM once this season|||Tdap 0.5 mL IM once, plus Hib 0.5 mL IM once
items.explanation: Give PCV20 0.5 mL IM once and do not follow it with PPSV23. PCV21 0.5 mL IM once is the other single-dose choice; PCV15 then PPSV23 at least 8 weeks later is the alternative, not a required conjugate-plus-polysaccharide series after PCV20. Also give MenACWY now and in 8 weeks, then every 5 years, a MenB series, influenza 0.5 mL IM, Tdap 0.5 mL IM once, and Hib 0.5 mL IM once. Fourteen days after splenectomy is an appropriate time. Recombinant zoster vaccine is for age 50 or older, or age 19 or older with immunosuppression; asplenia alone is not that indication. Takeaway: asplenia today means PCV20 or PCV21, MenACWY, MenB, Hib, influenza, and Tdap.

items.scenario: A 30-year-old woman with asthma requests her seasonal influenza vaccine. She uses albuterol 90 mcg, 2 inhalations as needed. Eating eggs has caused hives only, never anaphylaxis, wheezing, or a hospital visit.
items.question: Which plan is appropriate?
options: Give any age-appropriate influenza vaccine, 0.5 mL IM, and observe 15 minutes as for any vaccine
Use only an egg-free vaccine and observe her for 30 minutes
Defer vaccination until she is evaluated by an allergist
Give the vaccine but pretreat with diphenhydramine 50 mg
items.correctAnswer: Give any age-appropriate influenza vaccine, 0.5 mL IM, and observe 15 minutes as for any vaccine
items.explanation: ACIP says people with egg allergy may receive any age-appropriate influenza vaccine, egg-based or not, with no extra safety steps beyond those for any recipient. For this 30-year-old that is 0.5 mL IM once this season, then the usual 15-minute observation. Hives after eggs are not a reason for an egg-free product, a 30-minute watch, allergist clearance, or diphenhydramine 50 mg pretreatment. Asthma and albuterol use do not change that recommendation. Takeaway: egg allergy, including hives, is not a precaution that changes influenza vaccine choice or observation time.

items.topic: Egg allergy and influenza vaccine counseling
items.scenario: A 30-year-old woman with no chronic illnesses asks for an influenza vaccine. She says she is allergic to eggs. She is taking no medicines. Her immunization history is otherwise up to date.
items.question: Which counseling point is correct?
options: Egg allergy means she should skip influenza vaccine this season
She needs an egg-free product and a 30-minute observation
She can receive any age-appropriate influenza vaccine, 0.5 mL IM, with the usual 15-minute observation
Give half a dose, 0.25 mL IM, because of the egg allergy
items.correctAnswer: She can receive any age-appropriate influenza vaccine, 0.5 mL IM, with the usual 15-minute observation
items.explanation: Egg allergy alone does not contraindicate influenza vaccine and does not require an egg-free product, a longer observation, or a reduced dose. ACIP allows any vaccine appropriate for her age and health, given as 0.5 mL IM once this season, with the same 15-minute observation used for every recipient. Skipping the season leaves her unprotected. A 0.25 mL dose is not the adult dose and is not an egg-allergy adjustment. Takeaway: ask about severe allergy to a vaccine component, not eggs, before choosing the product.

items.topic: ACE inhibitor cough versus stage 1 blood pressure
items.scenario: A 42-year-old man refills lisinopril 20 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg daily. For the past week he has had a persistent dry cough that started after lisinopril. Blood pressure today is 130/85 mm Hg. He has no known drug allergies.
items.question: Which finding needs action before the refill is treated as routine?
options: Blood pressure of 130/85 mm Hg
Persistent dry cough after starting lisinopril
Request to refill atorvastatin
No known drug allergies
items.correctAnswer: Persistent dry cough after starting lisinopril
items.explanation: A new dry cough on lisinopril 20 mg daily is the adverse effect to act on; switch to an ARB such as losartan 50 mg daily if the cough is intolerable, rather than refilling the ACE inhibitor as routine. Blood pressure 130/85 mm Hg is stage 1 hypertension under the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline (130–139 or 80–89) and is above the treatment goal of below 130/80, so it needs planned follow-up, but it is not an emergency and it is not a normal reading. An atorvastatin refill and the absence of drug allergies need no urgent change. Takeaway: the cough is the immediate problem; 130/85 is above goal, not normal.

items.scenario: A 30-year-old man takes lisinopril 20 mg by mouth daily for hypertension. He feels well. Potassium is 5.8 mEq/L, creatinine is stable, and blood pressure is 130/85 mm Hg. He has no known drug allergies.
items.question: Which result should change therapy today?
options: No known drug allergies
Lisinopril dose of 20 mg daily by itself
Blood pressure of 130/85 mm Hg
Potassium of 5.8 mEq/L
items.explanation: Potassium 5.8 mEq/L on lisinopril 20 mg daily is hyperkalemia that can cause arrhythmia. Hold or reduce the ACE inhibitor, review salt substitutes and potassium-sparing drugs, and recheck potassium and creatinine promptly. Blood pressure 130/85 mm Hg is stage 1 hypertension and above the 2025 goal of below 130/80, so it still needs follow-up, but it is not the value that forces a same-day change and it is not a normal blood pressure. The 20 mg dose is a usual dose; the potassium, not the milligram strength, is the danger. Takeaway: ACE inhibitor plus potassium 5.8 means act today.

items.topic: ACE inhibitor cough, stage 1 blood pressure, and LDL
items.scenario: A 50-year-old man refills lisinopril 20 mg daily and atorvastatin 40 mg daily. He feels well except for a persistent dry cough. Blood pressure is 130/85 mm Hg and LDL cholesterol is 90 mg/dL.
items.question: Which finding should the pharmacist address before calling the visit routine?
options: LDL cholesterol of 90 mg/dL
Blood pressure of 130/85 mm Hg
Persistent dry cough
No medicine change of any kind
items.explanation: A persistent dry cough on lisinopril is an ACE-inhibitor effect. Offer a switch to an ARB, for example losartan 50 mg daily, if the cough is bothersome. Blood pressure 130/85 mm Hg is not normal: the 2025 AHA/ACC categories put 130–139 or 80–89 in stage 1 hypertension, and the treatment goal is below 130/80. It can be rechecked and adjusted at follow-up; it is not the acute issue. LDL 90 mg/dL is at a typical statin goal and does not need a same-day change. Takeaway: do not call 130/85 normal, and do not ignore an ACE-inhibitor cough.

items.topic: Orthostatic symptoms on an ACE inhibitor
items.scenario: A 60-year-old woman with hypertension and hyperlipidemia takes lisinopril 20 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg daily. She feels dizzy when she stands up quickly. Seated blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Lipids are at goal and she has no known drug allergies.
items.question: Which finding needs evaluation before she leaves?
options: Use of atorvastatin 20 mg daily
No known drug allergies
Dizziness when standing up quickly
Seated blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg
items.explanation: Dizziness on standing suggests orthostatic hypotension, which raises fall risk on lisinopril 20 mg daily. Check seated and standing blood pressures today and adjust therapy if the standing drop is confirmed. A seated reading of 130/80 mm Hg is not below the 2025 goal: the goal is under 130 and under 80, so this reading still needs planned follow-up. It is not, by itself, more urgent than orthostatic symptoms. Atorvastatin 20 mg daily and a lack of drug allergies do not explain the dizziness. Takeaway: measure orthostatic vital signs; do not file 130/80 as already at goal.

items.topic: New ACE inhibitor, cough, and stage 1 blood pressure
items.scenario: A 45-year-old woman is starting lisinopril 20 mg by mouth daily for hypertension. She reports a persistent dry cough, blood pressure 130/85 mm Hg, a father with hypertension, and a body mass index of 27 kg/m². She takes no other medicines and has no known drug allergies.
items.question: Which finding should change the plan today?
options: Body mass index of 27 kg/m²
Family history of hypertension
Blood pressure of 130/85 mm Hg
Persistent dry cough
items.explanation: A persistent dry cough is a reason to stop lisinopril 20 mg daily and use an ARB instead, such as losartan 50 mg daily. Blood pressure 130/85 mm Hg is stage 1 hypertension (130–139 or 80–89) and above the 2025 goal of below 130/80. It shows treatment is not finished, but it is an acceptable reason for follow-up rather than proof that the current reading is normal. Body mass index 27 kg/m² and a family history matter for long-term risk and do not require a same-day drug change. Takeaway: the cough changes today's drug; 130/85 is above goal, not a normal result.

items.topic: Uncontrolled hypertension with amlodipine edema and CKD
items.scenario: A 62-year-old man with hypertension and CKD has an eGFR of 48 mL/min/1.73 m². He takes amlodipine 10 mg daily and lisinopril 20 mg daily. Blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg and both ankles are swollen. Potassium is 4.4 mEq/L and creatinine is stable.
items.question: Which adjustment is most appropriate?
options: Stop lisinopril because he has CKD
Raise amlodipine to 15 mg daily
Add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg by mouth once daily
Raise lisinopril to 80 mg daily
items.correctAnswer: Add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg by mouth once daily
items.explanation: Blood pressure 150/90 mm Hg is above the 2025 goal of below 130/80. With eGFR 48, add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg daily: a thiazide-like diuretic is a first-line add-on and can lessen amlodipine edema. Keep lisinopril; an ACE inhibitor is indicated in CKD and a stable creatinine is not a reason to stop it. Raising lisinopril toward 40 mg can also lower blood pressure, but 80 mg exceeds the usual 40 mg daily maximum and does not treat the edema. Amlodipine has no 15 mg dose, and a higher dose would worsen swelling. Recheck creatinine, potassium, and blood pressure after the chlorthalidone start. Takeaway: at eGFR 48, add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg; do not stop the ACE inhibitor.

items.guideline: ADA consensus on hyperglycemic crises in adults with diabetes (2024)
items.scenario: A 30-year-old client with type 1 diabetes is treated for diabetic ketoacidosis with IV 0.9% sodium chloride and a regular insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour. After 6 hours, glucose is 240 mg/dL, pH is 7.26, anion gap is 18 mEq/L, and potassium is 4.1 mEq/L. The client is nauseated and not eating.
items.question: Which prescription should the nurse anticipate?
options: Stop the insulin infusion because glucose is below 250 mg/dL
Add dextrose to the IV fluid and continue the insulin infusion
Increase the insulin infusion to 0.2 units/kg/hour without dextrose
Switch to subcutaneous insulin and start a regular diet
items.correctAnswer: Add dextrose to the IV fluid and continue the insulin infusion
items.explanation: Glucose has fallen to 240 mg/dL, but pH 7.26 and an anion gap of 18 mEq/L show the ketoacidosis is still open. Add dextrose (D5) to the IV fluid and continue regular insulin at about 0.1 units/kg/hour until the gap closes, keeping potassium in the 4–5 mEq/L range. Stopping insulin because glucose is under 250 mg/dL lets ketogenesis resume. Raising the rate to 0.2 units/kg/hour without dextrose risks hypoglycemia while the gap is still 18. Subcutaneous insulin and a meal wait until the gap has closed and the client can eat; this client is still acidotic and nauseated. Takeaway: below 250 mg/dL, add dextrose and keep the insulin infusion going until the anion gap closes.
